title: USP10 promotes glioma stem cell maintenance and glioblastoma growth by antagonizing DTX3L-mediated SATB2 ubiquitination

paper_content.abstract: Special AT-rich sequence-binding protein 2 (SATB2) is a nuclear matrix-associated protein with a pivotal role in glioblastoma (GBM) progression. However, the mechanisms underpinning aberrant SATB2 expression remain elusive. Here, we identify the ubiquitin specific peptidase 10 (USP10) as a deubiquitinase and the deltex E3 ubiquitin ligase 3L (DTX3L) as a ubiquitin ligase of SATB2 in glioma stem cells (GSCs). USP10 and DTX3L regulate SATB2 ubiquitination at the K266 residue through mutually exclusive interactions and opposing activities. USP10, enriched in GSCs, is induced by transcription factor YY2. Knockdown of USP10 or overexpression of DTX3L markedly downregulates SATB2, resulting in the inhibition of GSC self-renewal and GBM growth, which can be rescued by the overexpression of SATB2. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of USP10 by Wu-5 effectively suppresses tumor growth. These findings highlight the antagonistic roles of USP10 and DTX3L in the regulation of GBM malignancy and propose USP10 as a potential therapeutic target.
paper_content.introduction:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most prevalent and devastating brain tumor in adults. The standard therapy for GBM is surgery followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Despite remarkable progress in the treatment of other solid tumors, the prognosis for GBM patients remains bleak, with the median survival of GBM patients remains less than 16 months1,2. The malignant features of GBM are thought to be attributable to glioma stem cells (GSCs), a fraction of stem cell-like cancer cells that possess extraordinary capabilities for rapid proliferation, self-renewal, and tumorigenesis3–5. These GSCs have been shown to play a significant role in the initiation, progression, recurrence and resistance to therapy of GBM6–9. Therefore, the development of novel therapeutic strategies targeting GSCs could provide significant insights that may enhance the efficacy of GBM treatments.

Special AT-rich sequence-binding protein 2 (SATB2) is a nuclear matrix-associated transcriptional factor that interacts with the nuclear matrix attachment regions of DNA, thereby regulating chromatin remodeling and gene transcription10–12. SATB2 recruits chromatin-remodeling proteins to the matrix attachment regions, either to activate or repress gene transcription11,13,14. This protein has been shown to play a crucial role in the progression of various cancer types, including hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, prostate cancer, triple-negative breast cancer, and others15–18. In GBM, SATB2 is overexpressed in GBM tissues when compared to low-grade gliomas, and it is predominantly enriched in GSCs19. Disruption of SATB2 significantly suppresses GSC proliferation and self-renewal19. Moreover, SATB2 plays a key role in the progression of GBM and significantly contributes to the development of resistance to temozolomide and radiation therapy19,20. However, the precise mechanisms underlying SATB2 dysregulation in GSCs remain unclear.

The ubiquitin-proteasome system constitutes the primary pathway for non-lysosomal proteolysis of intracellular proteins and is accountable for the degradation of more than 80% of cellular proteins21,22. Ubiquitination, which is a process that marks proteins for degradation, plays a crucial supportive role in this regulatory mechanism23. This process is reversible and can be mediated by a diverse group of enzymes known as deubiquitylating enzymes, or termed deubiquitinases24,25. USP10, a member of ubiquitin-specific protease (USP) family, is one such deubiquitinase26. It has been implicated in the development of various cancer types, including triple-negative breast cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and others27–29. Recent studies have indicated that disruption of USP10 can induce apoptosis in GBM cells and suppress proneural-to-mesenchymal transition, a critical process in GBM progression30,31. Deltex E3 ubiquitin ligase 3L (DTX3L) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase belonging to the deltex family32. This protein is associated with the occurrence and development of various cancer types, such as pancreatic cancer, cervical carcinoma, prostate cancer, and others33–35. However, the functional roles of USP10 and DTX3L in GSC biology remain largely enigmatic.

In this study, we identify that deubiquitinase USP10 and E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L function in concert to regulate the ubiquitination and stability of SATB2. Our data reveal that USP10 antagonizes DTX3L-mediated ubiquitination at the K266 residue, thereby stabilizing the SATB2 protein, which in turn contributes to the malignant phenotype of GSCs and the growth of GBM tumors. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of USP10 by a small molecule inhibitor, Wu-5, promotes SATB2 ubiquitination and thereby suppresses GSC proliferation, self-renewal, and tumor growth. These findings indicate that USP10 could be a promising target for patients with GBM.
paper_content.results:
USP10 and DTX3L interact with SATB2 in GSCs
To determine whether the SATB2 protein is degraded through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway or the lysosomal degradation pathway, we first checked the SATB2 protein levels in two patient-derived GSCs after blocked de novo protein synthesis using cycloheximide (CHX). GSCs were functionally validated as described in Methods. We found the SATB2 protein levels were decreased in a time-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. 1a). On the contrary, the protein levels of SATB2 were gradually increased after treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG-132 (Supplementary Fig. 1b). However, the protein levels of SATB2 remained unchanged after treatment with the lysosome inhibitor Bafilomycin A1 (Supplementary Fig. 1c). These results indicate that the degradation of SATB2 is mediated through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. To identify the potential deubiquitinases and ubiquitin ligases that regulate the ubiquitination and stability of SATB2, we performed mass spectrometry to analyze the SATB2-interacting proteins pulled down by the anti-Myc antibody from GSCs overexpressing Myc-tagged SATB2. Notably, among the top candidates of potential SATB2 binding partners, we identified the deubiquitinase USP10 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L (Fig. 1a, b and Supplementary Table. 1).

To validate the interactions between SATB2 and either USP10 or DTX3L, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (CoIP) experiments in HEK293T cells that were co-expressing SATB2 with a Myc tag and either USP10 or DTX3L with a Flag tag. CoIP assay revealed that exogenous USP10 or DTX3L was readily detected in exogenous SATB2 pull-down complexes and vice versa (Fig. 1c–f). These interactions were confirmed by showing that endogenous USP10 or DTX3L could be detected in immunoprecipitates of endogenous SATB2 in GSCs (Fig. 1g). To determine the specific region required for SATB2-USP10 or SATB2-DTX3L interaction, we generated various truncated mutants of SATB2-Myc, USP10-Flag, and DTX3L-Flag (Fig. 1h–j). CoIP assays showed that the central domain of SATB2 (amino acids 232–437) and the C-terminal USP domain of USP10 (amino acids 401–798) are required for interaction with each other (Fig. 1k, l). In addition, our results also showed that the central domain of SATB2 (amino acids 232–437) and the central domain of DTX3L (amino acids 201–554) are necessary for their interaction (Fig. 1m, n). Taken together, these data suggest that deubiquitinase USP10 and E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L interact with SATB2 in GSCs, suggesting that USP10 and DTX3L may regulate SATB2 stability.

USP10 and DTX3L are preferentially expressed by GSCs
Considering that SATB2 is reported to be preferentially expressed by GSCs19,20, we subsequently aimed to verify if USP10 and DTX3L are also predominantly expressed by GSCs within GBM. We initially examined the protein expression of USP10 and DTX3L in five pairs of matched GSCs and non-stem tumor cells (NSTCs). Immunoblot (IB) analysis showed that USP10 and DTX3L were preferentially expressed in GSCs compared with matched NSTCs (Fig. 2a). In addition, the enrichment of SATB2 in GSCs, as shown in Fig. 2a, aligns with the results of our previous study19. Moreover, qPCR analysis also revealed that the mRNA levels of USP10 and DTX3L were expressed at much higher levels in GSCs than in NSTCs (Fig. 2b, c). We next compared the expression between USP10 and DTX3L and the results showed that the expression of USP10 was significantly higher than DTX3L in GSCs (Fig. 2d). As deubiquitinase and E3 ubiquitin ligase exert antagonistic effects on protein stability, the higher expression of USP10 than DTX3L may account for the abundant expression of SATB2 in GSCs. Immunofluorescent staining revealed that USP10 and DTX3L were predominantly located in the cytoplasm, while SATB2 was primarily found in the nuclei in GSCs (Fig. 2e, f). This observation suggests that the cytoplasmic SATB2 may be translocated to the nucleus after deubiquitination. To verify this hypothesis, we first performed immunofluorescent staining of SATB2 in GSCs after treatment with MG-132 or DMSO. The results showed that MG-132 treatment induced nuclear export of SATB2 in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 1d). Furthermore, the ubiquitination assay detected ubiquitination of SATB2 in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus (Supplementary Fig. 1e). These results confirm that the cytoplasmic SATB2 is translocated to the nucleus following deubiquitination. Subsequently, to confirm the preferentially expression of USP10 and DTX3L by GSCs in GBM, we examined the expression pattern of USP10 and DTX3L in several human GBM tumors. Our data confirmed that USP10 and DTX3L were preferentially expressed in glioma cells expressing the GSC marker SOX2 (Fig. 2g, h and Supplementary Fig. 1f, g). Furthermore, USP10 and DTX3L were both co-localized with SATB2 in human primary GBMs (Fig. 2i, j and Supplementary Fig. 1h, i). Collectively, these data demonstrate that both USP10 and DTX3L are preferentially expressed by GSCs in human GBM tumors.

USP10 is required for GSC self-renewal and GSC-driven tumor growth
As USP10 is enriched in GSCs, we therefore explored the role of USP10 in GSC maintenance and GSC-driven tumor growth by using two independent shRNAs targeting USP10. As expected, lentiviral-mediated expression of two independent USP10 shRNAs significantly reduced USP10 protein levels in GSCs, which also induced a notable decrease of SATB2 protein levels (Fig. 3a). However, the mRNA levels of SATB2 remained unchanged after USP10 disruption (Fig. 3b). In contrast, SATB2 disruption did not alter USP10 mRNA or protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). Immunofluorescent staining also revealed that disruption of USP10 induced nuclear export of endogenous SATB2, which is consistent with our prediction (Supplementary Fig. 2c). FOXM1 is an important downstream target that mediates SATB2-promoted GSC proliferation and self-renewal19. We therefore investigated the impact of USP10 disruption on FOXM1 expression in GSCs, our results demonstrated that disrupting USP10 also reduced the mRNA and protein expression of FOXM1 (Supplementary Fig. 2d, e). However, this intervention had no effect on the expression of DTX3L (Supplementary Fig. 2d, e). As SATB2 is crucial for GSC maintenance, reduced expression of SATB2 protein by USP10 disruption may impact GSC functions. Our data demonstrated that silencing USP10 markedly inhibited GSC growth as detected by cell titer assay and reduced DNA replication as assayed by EdU incorporation assay (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 2f, g). In contrast, silencing USP10 had little effect on the growth of NSTCs (Supplementary Fig. 2h, i). Silencing USP10 also impaired GSC self-renewal as assessed by tumorsphere formation and in vitro limiting dilution assays (Fig. 3d–g). Consistently, silencing USP10 decreased the expression of the GSC marker SOX2 (Supplementary Fig. 2j). To verify whether the deubiquitinase activity of USP10 is required for GSC functions, we examined whether ectopic expression of wild-type (WT) or catalytically inactive mutant (C424A, CA) of USP10 could rescue the effects caused by USP10 disruption. We employed an additional USP10 shRNA that specifically targets the 3’ UTR of the endogenous USP10 mRNA (designated as shUSP10-3’) to achieve the knockdown of USP10 expression; thus, we were able to simultaneously silence endogenous USP10 and overexpress exogenous USP10 in GSCs. IB analysis showed that WT USP10, but not CA mutant, could rescue the decreased SATB2 protein levels caused by knockdown of endogenous USP10 (Supplementary Fig. 3a). In addition, ectopic expression of WT USP10, but not CA mutant, rescued the impaired GSC proliferation and self-renewal caused by endogenous USP10 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 3b-f). These results demonstrate that USP10 regulates SATB2 protein levels and GSC functions through its deubiquitinase activity.

To investigate the influence of USP10 on GSC-driven tumor growth in vivo, GSCs expressing shNT or shUSP10 were intracranially injected into the brains of immunodeficient mice. Animals bearing xenografts derived from GSCs expressing shUSP10 displayed extended survival and reduced tumor volumes than the control group (Fig. 3h, i). Immunofluorescent staining of Ki67 and SOX2 also demonstrated that disruption of USP10 markedly inhibited cell proliferation and reduced GSC population in GBM xenografts (Fig. 3j–m). Additionally, immunofluorescent staining of neuronal markers (MAP2 and TUBB3) and the astrocyte marker (GFAP) revealed that disruption of USP10 significantly increased the number of MAP2-, TUBB3-, and GFAP-positive cells (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). This finding demonstrates that USP10 disruption promotes the differentiation of GSCs in GBM xenografts. Furthermore, immunofluorescent staining confirmed a marked reduction in USP10 and SATB2 expression in xenografts expressing shUSP10 (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). Collectively, our data demonstrate that USP10 plays a critical role in promoting GSC self-renewal and GSC-driven tumor growth.

DTX3L impairs GSC self-renewal and GBM tumor growth
As the expression of DTX3L is much lower than USP10 in GSCs, we examined the role of DTX3L in GSCs by overexpressing of DTX3L. We found that overexpression of DTX3L reduced SATB2 protein levels, but this overexpression had no effect on SATB2 mRNA levels (Fig. 4a, b). In addition, the overexpression of DTX3L led to a reduction in FOXM1 expression, whereas it had no significant impact on USP10 expression and ubiquitination (Supplementary Fig. 5a–c). Based on these findings, we hypothesized that DTX3L may also exert an influence on GSC functions. Our results showed that overexpression of DTX3L significantly suppressed GSC growth and reduced DNA replication (Fig. 4c–e). Tumorsphere formation and in vitro limiting dilution assays demonstrated that overexpression of DTX3L impaired GSC self-renewal (Fig. 4f–i). Consistently, DTX3L overexpression also decreased the expression of SOX2 (Supplementary Fig. 5d). We also examined whether the DTX3L mutant (C561S and C564S, 2CS), which lacks E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, could regulate SATB2 protein levels and GSC functions. IB analysis indicated that overexpression of DTX3L 2CS did not result in the inhibition of SATB2 protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 5e). Moreover, DTX3L 2CS overexpression had only a weak promoting effect on ubiquitination of SATB2 (Supplementary Fig. 5f, g). Consistently, it showed no significant impact on GSC proliferation and self-renewal (Supplementary Fig. 5h–l). We subsequently investigated whether the overexpression of DTX3L influenced GSC-driven tumor growth in mouse brains. The results showed that mice bearing tumors derived from DTX3L overexpressing GSCs showed extended survival and reduced tumor masses (Fig. 4j, k). Additionally, tumors derived from DTX3L-overexpressing GSCs contained much fewer proliferative cells and GSC populations than those of the control tumors (Fig. 4l–o). Furthermore, DTX3L overexpression markedly promoted the differentiation of GSCs in GBM xenografts, as indicated by immunofluorescence of MAP2, TUBB3, and GFAP (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Immunofluorescent analysis further confirmed that DTX3L expression was elevated and SATB2 levels were reduced in xenografts derived from DTX3L-overexpressing GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Taken together, we conclude that DTX3L exerts inhibitory effects on GSC self-renewal and GBM growth.

DTX3L ubiquitinates SATB2, whereas USP10 mediates SATB2 deubiquitination
Our results have demonstrated that the E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L reduced the protein levels of SATB2, while the deubiquitinase USP10 was responsible for preserving SATB2 protein levels. To investigate the impact of DTX3L or USP10 on SATB2 protein stability, DTX3L-overexpressing or USP10 silencing GSCs were subjected to CHX treatment. IB analysis demonstrated that overexpression of DTX3L or disruption of USP10 led to destabilization of the SATB2 protein (Fig. 5a-d and Supplementary Fig. 7a–d). Given that SATB2 is degraded through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, we sought to verify that DTX3L and USP10 regulate the turnover of SATB2 via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. The results showed that MG-132 treatments inhibited the decreased protein levels of SATB2 induced by DTX3L overexpression or USP10 disruption (Fig. 5e, f). These data indicate that DTX3L and USP10 regulate SATB2 stability in a proteasome-dependent manner. To determine if DTX3L indeed catalyzes the polyubiquitination of SATB2, we co-expressed SATB2-Myc and DTX3L-Flag along with His-ubiquitin in HEK293T cells. As shown in Fig. 5g, overexpression of DTX3L promoted the ubiquitination of SATB2 in HEK293T cells. Consistently, overexpression of DTX3L promoted the ubiquitination of SATB2 in GSCs (Fig. 5h). Subsequently, we co-expressed SATB2-Myc and USP10-Flag along with His-ubiquitin in HEK293T cells. The results demonstrated that overexpression of USP10 reduced the ubiquitination of SATB2 in HEK293T cells (Fig. 5i). In addition, disruption of USP10 enhanced the ubiquitination of SATB2 in GSCs (Fig. 5j). Polyubiquitination can occur through seven different Lys residues on ubiquitin36. Accordingly, we generated ubiquitin vectors with intact K6, K11, K27, K29, K33, K48, or K63 linkages to examine which type of linkage on the SATB2 protein is modulated by DTX3L or USP10. As depicted in Fig. 5k, l, DTX3L robustly stimulated the assembly of K48-linked polyubiquitination, while showing no effect on other ubiquitin linkage types. Further analysis revealed that USP10 specifically disassembled K48-linked polyubiquitination without affecting other polyubiquitin chain types (Fig. 5m, n). These results indicate that DTX3L promotes K48-linked polyubiquitination of SATB2, whereas USP10 prevents this polyubiquitination type of SATB2.

As SATB2 interacts with both DTX3L and USP10 through its central domain, we speculated that DTX3L and USP10 may act as competitors for binding to SATB2. We therefore co-expressed DTX3L-HA and USP10-Flag with SATB2-Myc in HEK293T cells and the result showed that overexpression of USP10 suppressed the interaction between SATB2 and DTX3L (Supplementary Fig. 7e). Consistently, disruption of USP10 increased the endogenous interaction between SATB2 and DTX3L in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 7f). In addition, overexpression of USP10 prevented the reduced protein levels of SATB2 induced by DTX3L overexpression in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 7g). To confirm whether DTX3L and USP10 indeed function as an opposing pair of E3 ubiquitin ligase and deubiquitinase to regulate SATB2 ubiquitination and stability, we first co-expressed SATB2-Myc, DTX3L-HA, USP10-Flag with His-ubiquitin in HEK293T cells. CoIP assay revealed that overexpression of USP10 significantly reduced the ubiquitination of SATB2 induced by DTX3L overexpression (Supplementary Fig. 7h). Overexpression of USP10 also reduced the ubiquitination of endogenous SATB2 induced by DTX3L overexpression in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 7i, j). Furthermore, silencing DTX3L decreased the ubiquitination of endogenous SATB2 induced by USP10 disruption in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 7k, l). In vitro ubiquitination assays demonstrated that DTX3L directly promoted the ubiquitination of SATB2 (Supplementary Fig. 7m), whereas USP10 antagonized DTX3L-mediated SATB2 ubiquitination (Supplementary Fig. 7n). Functionally, overexpression of both DTX3L and USP10 prevented the inhibitory effect on GSC growth that was induced by DTX3L overexpression alone (Supplementary Fig. 7o). Conversely, simultaneous disruption of both DTX3L and USP10 attenuated the inhibitory effect on GSC growth that was triggered by USP10 disruption alone (Supplementary Fig. 7p). Collectively, we conclude that deubiquitinase USP10 maintains the protein levels of SATB2 by antagonizing DTX3L-mediated ubiquitination.

Overexpression of SATB2 rescues the effects caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression
Given that disruption of USP10 or overexpression of DTX3L reduced SATB2 protein levels, we next explored whether exogenous overexpression of SATB2 could rescue the effects induced by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression. The reduction in SATB2 levels caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression was corrected to match the levels of endogenous SATB2 in the control group by introducing additional SATB2 through exogenous overexpression (Fig. 6a, b and Supplementary Fig. 8a, b). Exogenous overexpression of SATB2 rescued the impaired GSC proliferation and self-renewal caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression (Fig. 6c-h and Supplementary Fig. 8c–j). Importantly, overexpression of SATB2 largely attenuated the increased survival of mice bearing xenografts derived from USP10 silencing or DTX3L overexpressing GSCs (Fig. 6i, j and Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). Consistently, overexpression of SATB2 restored the GSC-driven tumor growth impaired by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression (Fig. 6k, l and Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). Furthermore, immunofluorescent staining confirmed that overexpression of SATB2 restored in vivo cell proliferation impaired by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression, and rescued the reduced GSC population caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression (Fig. 6m–p and Supplementary Fig. 9e–h). Taken together, these data demonstrate that overexpression of SATB2 is able to rescue the effects caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression, indicating that USP10 and DTX3L regulate GSC self-renewal and GSC-driven tumor growth by controlling the protein levels of SATB2.

USP10 and DTX3L co-regulate the ubiquitination of SATB2 at K266
To pinpoint the lysine residues within human SATB2 protein that are regulated by USP10 or DTX3L, we generated a series of truncated SATB2 mutants and introduced them into HEK293T cells. Notably, among the various mutants, only the expression of the SATB2 mutant encompassing amino acids 232 to 437 exhibited a significant increase in response to USP10 overexpression (Fig. 7a). In addition, overexpression of DTX3L also inhibited the expression of this SATB2 mutant (amino acids 232–437), without affecting the expression of other mutants (Fig. 7b). Subsequently, we individually mutated all lysine residues within the SATB2 mutant (amino acids 232–437) to arginine. The results revealed that the SATB2-K266R mutant was uniquely unaffected by the overexpression of USP10 or DTX3L (Fig. 7c, d). Protein sequence alignment analysis revealed that the domain containing K266 within SATB2 protein is highly conserved across seven distinct species (Fig. 7e). To confirm the ubiquitination site of SATB2, we performed mass spectrometry to analyze the immunoprecipitated SATB2 proteins from HEK293T cells co-expressing SATB2-Myc and His-ubiquitin. The results showed that ubiquitin moieties were exclusively detected on residue K266 (Fig. 7f), confirming that the K266 site is the ubiquitination site of SATB2. To ascertain whether K266 of SATB2 is regulated by USP10 or DTX3L in GSCs, we mutated K266 within the full-length SATB2 and introduced this mutant into GSCs. The results confirmed that the expression of the SATB2-K266R mutant was unaffected by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression in GSCs (Fig. 7g–j). Additionally, to verify whether DTX3L directly catalyzes the ubiquitination of SATB2 at the K266 residue, we co-expressed Myc-tagged WT SATB2 or K266R (KR) mutant SATB2 with DTX3L-Flag and His-ubiquitin in HEK293T cells. CoIP experiment demonstrated that overexpression of DTX3L promoted SATB2 ubiquitination, while it had no obvious effect on the ubiquitination of SATB2-K266R mutant (Fig. 7k). Furthermore, overexpression of USP10 reduced SATB2 ubiquitination and showed no effect on the ubiquitination of the SATB2-K266R mutant (Fig. 7l). Collectively, these data reveal that the K266 within SATB2 is crucial for the deubiquitination and ubiquitination by USP10 and DTX3L.

YY2 activates USP10 transcription in GSCs
Given the abundant expression of USP10 mRNA by GSCs, we explored the mechanism of increased USP10 transcription in GSCs. We analyzed the human USP10 promoter region (−2,000 to +100) using JASPAR database to predict transcription factors that regulate USP10 transcription. PBX homeobox 2 (PBX2), YY2 transcription factor (YY2), and nuclear factor, interleukin 3 regulated (NFIL3) were the top three transcription factors with the highest scores (Supplementary Table 2). Additionally, we have enumerated the potential binding motifs for each of these transcription factors (Supplementary Table 2). We next silenced each of these transcription factors and found that only the disruption of YY2 inhibited the mRNA expression of USP10 (Supplementary Fig. 10a–c). IB analysis revealed that disruption of YY2 reduced USP10 and SATB2 protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 10d). Moreover, IB analysis demonstrated that YY2 and USP10 were preferentially expressed in GSCs compared with matched NSTCs (Supplementary Fig. 10e). To examine whether YY2 and USP10 are colocalized in GBM, we examined the expression pattern of YY2 and USP10 in human GBM tissues. Immunofluorescent staining demonstrated that YY2 was co-localized with USP10 in human GBM specimens (Supplementary Fig. 10f, g). Further analysis confirmed that YY2 was indeed enriched in nuclei of glioma cells expressing the GSC marker SOX2 (Supplementary Fig. 10h, i). To test whether YY2 directly stimulates the transcription of USP10, we performed a luciferase reporter assay. The results revealed that overexpression of YY2 increased USP10 promoter activity (Supplementary Fig. 10j). However, the activating effect by YY2 was completely eliminated upon mutation of the YY2-binding site within the USP10 promoter (Supplementary Fig. 10j). Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay confirmed that YY2 was present on its own binding site on the proximal USP10 promoter in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 10k). Taken together, these results suggest that YY2 activates USP10 transcription by binding to USP10 promoter in GSCs.

USP10 inhibitor Wu-5 suppresses GSC self-renewal and GSC-driven tumor growth
To evaluate the therapeutic potential of USP10 in GBM, we investigated whether pharmacologic inhibition of USP10 by a small molecule inhibitor named Wu-5 could impact GSCs and GSC-driven tumor growth. Cell viability assay revealed that 8 and 16μM Wu-5 dose-dependently inhibited GSC growth, whereas lower concentrations (2 and 4μM) showed no significant effect (Fig. 8a). Wu-5 treatment also impaired GSC self-renewal and downregulated SOX2 expression in a dose-dependent manner (8 and 16μM) (Fig. 8b–e and Supplementary Fig. 11a). Furthermore, Wu-5 (8 and 16μM) dose-dependently induced GSC apoptosis, as demonstrated by the elevated levels of apoptotic markers Cleaved Caspase-7 and Cleaved PARP (Supplementary Fig. 11b). As expected, Wu-5 treatment reduced SATB2 protein levels in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Fig. 8f and Supplementary Fig. 11c). We also observed that Wu-5 treatment reduced USP10 protein levels in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Fig. 8f and Supplementary Fig. 11c), which is in line with the findings from previous research37,38. Nonetheless, treatment with 8 and 16μM Wu-5 had no impact on SATB2 and USP10 mRNA levels (Fig. 8g and Supplementary Fig. 11d). Consistently, Wu-5 treatment at 8 and 16μM dose-dependently increased the ubiquitination of SATB2 in GSCs (Fig. 8h). To determine whether SATB2 overexpression can rescue the effects of Wu-5 treatment on GSC maintenance, we transduced GSCs with SATB2-Myc and treated them with Wu-5 (16μM). IB analysis showed that ectopic SATB2 expression restored SATB2 to endogenous levels, which had been reduced by Wu-5 treatment (Supplementary Fig. 11e). Importantly, restoring SATB2 to endogenous levels significantly rescued the Wu-5-induced impairment of GSC proliferation and self-renewal (Supplementary Fig. 11f–j). These data indicate that Wu-5 treatment inhibits GSC maintenance via the USP10-SATB2 axis. We then assessed the therapeutic effects of Wu-5 on mice bearing GSC-derived xenografts. Consistent with our in vitro findings, Wu-5 treatment effectively prolonged the survival of mice bearing GSC-derived tumors and reduced tumor volumes in mouse brains (Fig. 8i–k). Notably, no significant alterations in body weight were observed throughout the treatment period (Supplementary Fig. 12a, b). Wu-5 administration also significantly reduced Ki67-positive proliferative cells and SOX2-positive GSC populations in tumors (Fig. 8l–o). Moreover, immunofluorescent staining for MAP2, TUBB3, and GFAP revealed that Wu-5 robustly promoted GSC differentiation in GBM xenografts (Supplementary Fig. 12c–f). Additionally, Wu-5 treatment reduced SATB2 and USP10 in xenografts (Supplementary Fig. 12g–j). To confirm whether Wu-5 can penetrate the blood-brain barrier, we intraperitoneally administered Wu-5 or DMSO to BALB/c nude mice and subsequently detected Wu-5 in mouse brain tissues by LC-MS/MS. The results demonstrated that Wu-5 concentrations reached an average of 673 ng/g tissue in the brains of mice treated with Wu-5 for 2 hours, whereas Wu-5 levels were very low and nearly undetectable in the brains of DMSO-treated controls (Supplementary Fig. 12k). Together, these data suggest that pharmacological inhibition of USP10 significantly suppresses GSC self-renewal and tumor growth via promoting SATB2 destabilization, suggesting that that targeting USP10 may effectively improve GBM treatment.
paper_content.methods:
Tissues and cells
Human GBM specimens in this study were collected from the Center for Neurological Disease Research at Taihe Hospital in accordance with an Institutional Research Ethics Committee-approved protocol. Informed consent was obtained from all subjects. GSCs and NSTCs were kindly provided by Dr. Jeremy N. Rich (University of Pittsburgh) and Dr. Shideng Bao (Cleveland Clinic). GSCs and NSTCs were isolated from primary GBM tumors or patient-derived xenografts and functionally characterized19,50,51. In brief, cells were dissociated from tumors using the Papain Dissociation Kit (Worthington Biochemical, Cat# LK003150) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The isolated cells were recovered overnight in the Neurobasal-A medium (Thermo Fisher, Cat# A2477501), supplemented with B27 (Thermo Fisher, Cat# 12587010), 20 ng/ml EGF (Gold biotechnology, Cat# 1150-04-1000), 20 ng/ml bFGF (PrimeGene, Cat# 104-02), 2 mM L-glutamine (Thermo Fisher, Cat# 35050061) and 1 mM sodium pyruvate (Thermo Fisher, Cat# 11360070). Cells were then sorted by FACs using a PE-conjugated anti-CD133 antibody (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat# 130-113-108) and a FITC-conjugated anti-CD15 antibody (BD Biosciences, Cat# 347423), to obtain the GSC population (CD15+/CD133+) and the NSTC population (CD15-/CD133-). The cancer stem cell characteristics of isolated GSCs were validated by expression of GSC markers, including SOX2, OLIG2, L1CAM, and CD133, and functional assays, including serial tumorsphere formation, induced differentiation and tumor propagation assays. GSCs were cultured in the Neurobasal-A medium with supplements as described above. NSTCs were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (VivaCell, Cat# C04001-500) to maintain the differentiation characteristics. HEK293T cells (ATCC, Cat# CRL-3216) were cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS. Information on patients’ sex was collected through self-reporting. Sex was not incorporated into the study design or analysis, as investigating potential sex-specific effects was outside the scope of this research. Patient information for the GBM specimens are listed in Supplementary Table 3.

Mass spectrometry analysis
SATB2 and its interacting proteins were co-immunoprecipitated from cell lysates of GSCs overexpressing SATB2-Myc or HEK293T cells overexpressing SATB2-Myc and His-ubiquitin. The precipitates were then analyzed by mass spectrometry at BGI-Tech to identify SATB2-interacting proteins and at Nanjing Newtop Biotech (Nanjing, China) to identify ubiquitinated sites on SATB2. Briefly, cell lysates were incubated with anti-Myc antibody (Proteintech, 60003-2-Ig) or IgG, along with protein A/G Plus agarose beads (Santa Cruz, sc-2003), overnight at 4°C. The SATB2-Myc protein complex captured by the beads is eluted, boiled and separated on SDS-PAGE, and stained by Coomassie blue staining. The visible band was cut, treated with acetonitrile, and then trypsinized.

For the identification of SATB2 binding proteins, peptides from both the experimental group and a control IgG group were extracted and separated. The peptides separated by liquid phase chromatography were ionized by a nano ESI source and then passed to a tandem mass spectrometer (Orbitrap Fusion Lumos, Thermo Fisher) for DDA (data-dependent acquisition) mode detection. The main parameters were set as follows: ion source voltage, 2 kV; MS1 scanning range, 350–1500 m/z; MS1 resolution, 60,000; MS2 starting m/z, 100; MS2 resolution, 15,000. The ion screening conditions for MS2 fragmentation were: charge 2+ to 6+, and the top 30 parent ions with the peak intensity exceeding 20,000. The ion fragmentation mode was HCD, and the fragment ions were detected in the Orbitrap. The dynamic exclusion time was set to 30 s. The AGC was set to 1E5 for MS1 and 2E4 for MS2. For protein identification, experimental MS/MS data were matched against theoretical MS/MS data from a protein database. The raw MS data were converted into a peak list and searched against the UniProt database using Mascot (version 2.3.02). The search was performed using an mgf file as input against a pre-constructed database. The Mascot parameters were set as follows: Enzyme: Trypsin; Peptide mass tolerance: 10 ppm; Fragment mass tolerance: 0.02 Da; Fixed modifications: Carbamidomethyl (C); Variable modifications: Oxidation (M), Gln->pyro-Glu (N-term Q), Deamidated (NQ), Phospho (ST), Phospho (Y); Max missed cleavages: 1; Instrument type: ESI-FTICR. The search results were pre-processed and rescored using Percolator to improve the matching accuracy. The output was then filtered at a 1% false discovery rate (FDR) at the spectral level (PSM-level FDR ≤ 0.01) to obtain a list of significantly identified spectra and peptides.

For the identification of ubiquitinated sites on SATB2, peptides from both the experimental group and a control IgG group were extracted. The peptide samples were then separated and analyzed by a Q-Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher) operating in DDA mode. The total analysis time was 60 min in positive ion mode. The full scan MS1 spectra were collected over the m/z range of 350–1800 with a resolution of 60,000 at 200 m/z, an AGC target of 3e6, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. For MS2 acquisition, the top 20 most intense precursor ions from each full scan were selected for fragmentation. The MS2 spectra were acquired with a resolution of 15,000 at 200 m/z, an AGC target of 1e5, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. HCD was used as the fragmentation mode with an isolation window of 1.6 m/z and a normalized collision energy of 28. For protein identification, experimental MS/MS data were matched against theoretical MS/MS data from a protein database. The raw MS data were searched against the UniProt database using MaxQuant (version 2.4.14.0). The MaxQuant parameters were set as follows: Enzyme: Trypsin; Precursor Tolerance (main search): 4.5 ppm; Precursor Tolerance (first search): 20 ppm; MS/MS tolerance: 20 ppm; Fixed modifications: Carbamidomethyl (C); Variable modifications: Oxidation (M), Acetyl (Protein N-term), GlyGly (K). After database searching, the mass spectrometry data were filtered using the following criteria: PSM FDR ≤ 0.01, Site FDR ≤ 0.01, and Protein FDR ≤ 0.01 for peptide, modification site, and protein identification, respectively. To ensure the quality of modified peptide identifications, additional filters were applied, including a Modified Peptide Score ≥ 40 and the presence of at least one unmodified peptide (Unmodified peptides ≥ 0). A modification site was considered confidently localized when its localization probability was ≥ 0.75.

Intracranial tumor formation and treatment
BALB/c-Nude mice were purchased from Hunan Slack Jingda Experimental Animal (Changsha, China). Male or female BALB/c nude mice at 6–7 weeks were used and housed in the animal facility of the laboratory animal center at Huazhong Agricultural University. Mice were maintained at 22–24°C and 40–70% humidity with a 12 h light/12 h dark schedule. Sex was not incorporated into the study design or analysis, as investigating potential sex-specific effects was outside the scope of this research. 50,000 GSCs were implanted into the right cerebral cortex at a depth of 3.5 mm to establish intracranial xenografts. Mice were maintained until neurological signs appeared (survival analysis). Neurological signs included hunched posture, gait changes, lethargy, and weight loss. For the drug treatment, Wu-5 (7.5 mg/kg; TargetMol, Cat# T77763) was dissolved in DMSO (Santa Cruz, sc-358801). 7 days post-GSC transplantation, mice were treated with Wu-5 or vehicle control 6 days per week and maintained until the appearance of neurological signs (survival analysis). The maximum tumor burden permitted by the ethics committee is 1.2 cm in diameter for mice, and the tumor weight must not exceed 10% of the body weight. No animals exceeded these limits in this study.

Cell viability, tumorsphere formation, and in vitro limiting dilution assays
For the cell viability assay, cells were plated into a 96-well plate at a density of 1,500 cells/well. Cell viability was measured by CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay kit (Promega, Cat# G7572) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For the tumorsphere formation assay, 1,500 GSCs were seeded into each well of a 96-well plate. The number of tumorspheres in each well was recorded, and the diameter of tumorspheres was analyzed on the sixth day after cell seeding. Tumorsphere images were collected by using the ECHO Revolve RVL-100. For the in vitro limiting dilution assay, a gradient number of GSCs (0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 cells/well) with 24 replicates per number were plated into a 96-well plate. The presence of tumorspheres was recorded on day 6, and the self-renewal capacity of GSCs was analyzed using ELDA software available at http://bioinf.wehi.edu.au/software/elda/.

EdU incorporation assay
For the EdU incorporation assay, EdU solution was added to the GSC medium for 2 hours, then cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). EdU in cells was stained using the BeyoClick™ EdU-594 kit (Beyotime, Cat# C0078) following the manufacturer’s protocol. The percentage of EdU-positive cells to total cells was obtained to indicate proliferation.

DNA constructs and lentiviral production
Lentiviral constructs expressing shRNAs against human USP10, DTX3L, YY2, and a non-targeting shRNA were cloned into pLKO.1-puro vector (Addgene, Cat# 8453). The shRNA sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 4 and were synthesized by GeneCreate (Wuhan, China). USP10-Flag, DTX3L-Flag, DTX3L-HA, and SATB2-Myc were generated by cloning their open reading frame (ORF) into the pLVX-EF1α-IRES-Neo (MiaoLing Bio, Cat# P23885) or pLVX-EF1α-IRES-Puro vector (MiaoLing Bio, Cat# P0405). SATB2 (Full length) and its truncated mutants were generated by cloning the corresponding sequences into pcDNA3.1-Myc vector (Thermo Fisher, Cat# V85520). USP10 (Full length) and its truncated mutants were generated by cloning the corresponding sequences into pcDNA3.1-Flag vector, which was modified from pcDNA3.1-Myc vector. DTX3L (Full length) and its truncated mutants were generated by cloning the corresponding sequences into the pcDNA3.1-Flag vector. Point mutations were generated by site-directed mutagenesis. The SATB2 (232-437aa) mutants K233R, K266R, K350R, K373R and K400R were generated using SATB2 (232-437aa) as the template and cloned into pcDNA3.1-Myc vector. The SATB2 K266R-Myc was generated using SATB2-Myc as the template and cloned into the pLVX-EF1α-IRES-Puro vector. The USP10 CA-Flag was generated where C424 was mutated to A and cloned into the pLVX-EF1α-IRES-Neo vector. The DTX3L C561/564S-HA was generated, where C561 and C564 were mutated to S and cloned into the pLVX-EF1α-IRES-Neo vector. The USP10 ORF vector for cloning was kindly provided by Dr. Bo Yang and Dr. Hong Zhu (Zhejiang University). The pCDH-His-Ub-MSCV, pCDH-His-K48Ub-MSCV, and pCDH-His-K63Ub-MSCV plasmids were kindly provided by Dr. Xiuxing Wang (Nanjing Medical University). The pCDH-His-K6 Ub-MSCV, pCDH-His-K11 Ub-MSCV, pCDH-His-K27 Ub-MSCV, pCDH-His-K29 Ub-MSCV, and pCDH-His-K33 Ub-MSCV were generated using His-Ub as the template. Lentiviral particles were generated in HEK293T cells by co-transfection of lentiviral vector, pCL-VSVG (Addgene, Cat# 1733) and psPAX2 (Addgene, Cat# 12260) using a standard calcium phosphate transfection method. The viruses collected from the media were then concentrated through ultracentrifugation.

Quantitative Real-Time PCR (qPCR)
Total cellular RNA was extracted using RNAiso Plus (Takara, Cat# 9109) and reverse transcribed into cDNA using PrimeScript™ RT Master Mix (Takara, Cat# RR036A). qPCR was conducted on a 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) by using TaqPro Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Cat# Q712-02). Target RNA abundance was indicated by the cycle threshold (Ct) value and calculated using the 2−ΔΔCT method. qPCR primers were synthesized by GeneCreate (Wuhan, China). qPCR data were collected by using the Applied Biosystems 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR System. Sequences of qPCR primers were as follows: 18S rRNA, forward 5’-CTACCACATCCAAGGAAGGCA-3’, reverse 5’-TTTTTCGTCACTACCTCCCCG-3’; USP10, forward 5’-GAGGG CACAGCTACCAACG-3’, reverse 5’-AGGGGAGATATGGCGGGAG-3’; DTX3L, forward 5’-AGCACCAAATACTTGTTGACGA-3’, reverse 5’-CAC CAGACGGTGTTTCTGCTT-3’; SATB2, forward 5’-GGAGAACGACAGCG AGGAA-3’, reverse 5’-CCGATGTATTGCTTTGCCTAGT-3’; FOXM1, forward 5’-ATACGTGGATTGAGGACCACTA-3’, reverse 5’-TCCAATGT CAAGTAGCGGTTG-3’; YY2, forward 5’-GGTGGGCTATTGCGACTCAG-3’, reverse 5’-GCTCGTCTTCAATGCT ATCCG-3’; PBX2, forward 5’- GACAACTCCATCGAACACTCG-3’, reverse 5’-ACATGGGTCGTGAA CTCATTAC-3’; NFIL3, forward 5’-AGAACAAACTAATTGCACTGGGA-3’, reverse 5’-GCTCGTCCACAAATGAACTCAC-3’.

Immunoblot (IB) analysis and co-immunoprecipitation (CoIP)
For IB analysis, cells were lysed in RIPA lysis buffer containing protease inhibitors for 30 minutes and centrifuged at 15,000 g for 15 min. The protein samples were separated by SDS-PAGE gels, transferred to PVDF membranes, and blocked with 5% non-fat milk for 1 hour. Blots were incubated with primary antibodies overnight, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies. Immunoreactivity was detected by Ultra-sensitive ECL chemiluminescent substrate (Biosharp, Cat# BL523B) with the Bio-Rad ChemiDoc XRS+ Imaging System. For CoIP, cells were lysed in IP lysis buffer containing protease inhibitors for 30 minutes and centrifuged at 15,000 g for 15 min. Protein lysates were incubated with primary antibodies and protein A/G Plus agarose beads (Santa Cruz, Cat# sc-2003) overnight at 4°C. Then, the beads were washed with IP wash buffer 3 times. The precipitated proteins were boiled and subjected to IB analysis. Antibodies and dilutions are listed in Supplementary Table 5. Uncropped images are provided in the Source Data file.

Ubiquitination assay
Cells were treated with MG-132 (20µM; GLPBIO, Cat# GC10383) for 6 hours and then lysed in IP buffer containing protease inhibitors. CoIP was performed with the indicated antibody and protein A/G Plus agarose beads (Santa Cruz, Cat# sc-2003) overnight at 4°C. The precipitated proteins were denaturized and released from beads by boiling in SDS loading buffer for 10 minutes. Protein lysates were detected by IB analysis with the anti-ubiquitin antibody (Biolegend, Cat# 646302).

In vitro ubiquitination assay
His-SATB2, His-DTX3L, GST-USP10, and His-ubiquitin proteins were expressed and purified in BL21 (DE3) E. coli. In vitro ubiquitination assay was performed at 37°C for 2 hours in a 30-μl reaction buffer (40 mM Tris pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 2 mM DTT) containing 40 nM His/GST-UBA1 (E1, TargetMol, Cat# TMPY-02840), 300 nM GST-UBE2D1 (E2, TargetMol, Cat# TMPJ-00999), 4 μM His-ubiquitin, 120 nM His-SATB2, 120 nM His-DTX3L, 100 nM GST-USP10, and 5 mM ATP (Beyotime, Cat# D7378). The reactions were terminated by the addition of SDS loading buffer, and the reaction products were analyzed by IB analysis.

Immunofluorescent staining
Immunofluorescent staining was performed in tissues or cultured cells. GBM xenografts were collected from mice when neurological signs appeared after GSC transplantation. Human GBM samples were collected from patients through surgical resection. Briefly, tumor sections or cultured cells were fixed in 4% PFA for 10 minutes and permeabilized with 0.3% Triton X-100. The slides were then incubated with primary antibody at 4°C overnight, followed by fluorescent second antibody at room temperature for 2 hours. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI for 10 minutes, and sections were subjected to microscopy using a Leica DMi8 microscope or an Andor confocal spinning disk on a Nikon inverted microscope Eclipse Ti-E. Antibodies and dilutions are listed in Supplementary Table 5.

Luciferase reporter and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays
The promoter region (−2000 to +100) of human USP10 was inserted into the pGL3-basic vector (Promega, Cat# E1751) to generate the USP10 reporter construct. The mutant USP10 reporter construct was generated, where GGC (+27 to +29) was mutated to AAT and cloned into the pGL3-basic vector. Flag-YY2 was generated by cloning its ORF into the pLVX-EF1α-IRES-Puro vector (MiaoLing Bio, Cat# P0405). For the luciferase reporter assay, cells were co-transfected with USP10 reporter plasmid or mutant plasmid, Flag-YY2 overexpression vector, and pRL internal control vector (Promega, Cat# E2231). Luciferase activities were detected 48 hours post-transfection using the Dual-Luciferase® Reporter Assay System (Promega, Cat# E1910) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, with the BioTek Cytation5 plate reader. Firefly luciferase activities were normalized to Renilla. For the ChIP assay, cells were fixed with 1% formaldehyde for 10 minutes, terminated with glycine, and washed 3 times with cold PBS. Then, chromatin lysates were sonicated to break the chromatin, and the supernatant was collected after centrifugation. The sonicated lysates were pre-cleared with protein A/G Plus agarose beads (Santa Cruz, sc-2003) and immunoprecipitated by the indicated antibody or control IgG in the presence of salmon sperm DNA and BSA overnight. Beads were washed and then decrosslinked at 65°C for 12 hours. DNA was purified with a DNA purification kit and analyzed by PCR analysis. ChIP primers were synthesized by GeneCreate (Wuhan, China). Gel images were acquired by using the Tanon MINI Space 2000 Imaging System (Shanghai, China). The primers used are detailed below: forward 5’-CCGATGCGAGTGTGTATGTG-3’; reverse 5’-TATACTGCGGGCTGTG GAG-3’. Antibodies are shown in Supplementary Table 5. Uncropped images are provided in the Source Data file.

Statistics and reproducibility
All data are presented as the mean ± SD from at least three samples or experiments per data point. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 10 software. Two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test was used to evaluate the statistical significance for two groups. One-way ANOVA analysis followed by Tukey’s test was used to examine the statistical significance for more than two groups. For quantification with two groups and the groups with subgroups, two-way ANOVA analysis followed by Sidak’s test was used to evaluate statistical significance. For quantification with more than two groups and the groups with subgroups, two-way ANOVA analysis followed by Tukey’s test was used to evaluate statistical significance. Data were normally distributed. A log-rank test was used to determine the statistical significance of Kaplan-Meier survival curves. For all statistical tests, p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Precise experimental details are described in the figure legends.

Ethics statement
All animal procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Animal Experimental Ethics Committee of Huazhong Agricultural University. The use of clinical specimens was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Taihe Hospital (the Affiliated Hospital of Hubei University of Medicine, Shiyan, China).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Dysregulation of protein homeostasis is a well-established driver of cancer. In this manuscript, Guo et al. uncover a
regulatory mechanism involving an E3 ubiquitin ligase and a deubiquitinase (DUB) that modulates the stability of SATB2, a
key protein implicated in glioblastoma (GBM) progression. The authors demonstrate that in glioma stem cells (GSCs), the
elevated expression of USP10 relative to DTX3L stabilizes SATB2. This stabilization promotes the downstream effects of
SATB2, including increased FOXM1 expression, which supports GSC maintenance and GBM growth. Conversely, the
knockdown of USP10 or overexpression of DTX3L reduces FOXM1 levels and GSC proliferation, an effect rescued by
SATB2 overexpression. Finally, the study reports that the USP10 inhibitor, Wu-5, significantly inhibits GSC-driven tumor
growth.
While the manuscript presents some novel findings, its overall impact is moderate. Several key issues need to be addressed
to substantiate the authors' claims and enhance the rigor of the study.
Major points:
1.The authors rely solely on MG132 to assess proteasome-mediated degradation of SATB2. However, lysosomal
degradation cannot be excluded based on the data provided. To address this, additional experiments using lysosomal
inhibitors such as Bafilomycin A1 should be performed. This will help delineate the relative contributions of proteasomal and
lysosomal pathways to SATB2 degradation.
2.The manuscript proposes that "cytoplasmic SATB2 may be translocated to the nucleus after deubiquitination." However,
this claim is inadequately supported. Figures 2e and 2f indicate that while USP10 and DTX3L are cytoplasmic, SATB2 is
primarily in nucleus, suggesting that deubiquitinated SATB2 might enter the nucleus. To substantiate this hypothesis, the
authors should conduct additional experiments: treating GSCs with MG132 to inhibit the degradation of ubiquitinated
SATB2 and assess its localization through immunofluorescence; Isolating cytoplasm and nucleus fractions following MG132
treatment, perform SATB2 immunoprecipitation, and probe with an anti-ubiquitin antibody to determine its ubiquitination
status in each compartment.
3.The ubiquitination assays presented in Figures 5g and 5k have design flaws that hinder the interpretation of results. The
authors used myc-antibody to perform immunoprecipitation and then blot with His antibody to detect ubiquitinated SATB2.
Considering that many E3 ligases co-expressing with Ub show strong auto-ubiquitination, especially here SATB2 interacts
with DTX3L, thus this result couldn’t differentiate the ubiquitinated SATB2 and auto-ubiquitinated DTX3L which binds to
SATB2. In addition, DTX3L and SATB2 share similar molecular weight. Western Blot with anti-SATB2 could solve this
problem. The authors should show the intact Ub blot, not the part above 95 kDa only. This specific point applies to the rest of
ubiquitination blot.
4.Identifying the key ubiquitinated sites of SATB2 using mass spectrometry analysis helps strength the conclusion that K266
is the ubiquitination/deubiquitination site of DTX3L and USP10. Regarding the identification of the ubiquitin chain type on
SATB2 by DTX3L, K48 and K63 ubiquitin mutations are not enough as they can’t excluded other 5 types of Ub chains. The
authors should include all types of lysine mutated ubiquitin variants to provide a comprehensive understanding of the
ubiquitin chain architecture.
5.The molecular mechanism underlying SATB2 degradation by Wu-5 treatment remains unclear. Both USP10 inhibition and
the downregulation of USP10 protein level could lead to increased ubiquitination of SATB2 by DTX3L, ultimately resulting in
its degradation. The authors should provide further clarification to distinguish between these possibilities.
Minor points:
1. The manuscript contains numerous typos that affect its readability. Examples include:
Page 5, Line 96: "……refgulatory mechanism……" Page 6, Line 126: "……SATB2-interating……"
The authors should carefully proofread the manuscript.
2. It is unclear which shUSP10 was used in Figure 5C-D. The authors should clearly indicate the shUSP10 used in the
experiments.
3. In Figure S2a, "shUSP10-1" appeared twice. It is unclear whether the authors performed the immunofluorescence
experiments twice using the same construct or if this is a labeling error.
4. Misuse of tenses detracts from the quality of the manuscript.
For instance: Page 6, Line 119: "……first check……" should be revised to "……first checked……."
5. The abbreviation "NSTCs" (Non-stem tumor cells) is introduced without explanation. The authors should define this term
upon its first use in the manuscript to ensure clarity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, Guo et al. investigated the mechanisms regulating SATB2 expression in glioma stem cells (GSCs) and,
for the first time, identified USP10 as a deubiquitinase and DTX3L as an E3 ligase for SATB2 in GSCs. The authors also
determined that K266 is the lysine residue regulated by these two proteins. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated that
USP10 is essential for GSC self-renewal and tumorigenesis in vivo, with its effects being rescued by the overexpression of
SATB2. The authors identified YY2 as the upstream transcription factor mediating USP10 upregulation in GSCs. Lastly, they
assessed the therapeutic potential of the USP10 inhibitor Wu-5 in a glioma mouse xenograft model, highlighting the
translational promise of this project. Overall, this study is well-designed with appropriate controls. The data are of high
quality and robust in supporting the main conclusions, though additional evidence is needed in certain areas, as outlined
below. The manuscript is well-prepared, with clear descriptions and detailed information. Moreover, the authors need to
address the following comments to further strengthen this study. The current enthusiasm for this manuscript is high.
1. Fig. 2h-j and Fig. S1c-f: The authors showed that USP10 and DTX3L are expressed in more than 80% of SOX2+ or
SATB2+ cells in clinical GBM samples. However, this does not establish that these genes are preferentially expressed in
SOX2+ cells, as SOX2- cells were not included for comparison. Moreover, in Fig. S1c-f, only three replicates were included
for each group. Were these replicates derived from different fields of the same patient sample or from different patients? The
authors should include data from more fields (typically >10) as well as all analyzed patient samples. The same question
applies to Fig. S7f-i.
2. To support their conclusion that USP10, DTX3L, and SATB2 are preferentially expressed in GSCs, the authors should
analyze published single-cell RNA-seq datasets of clinical glioblastoma (GBM) samples and compare the expression of
these genes across different GBM cellular states. Additionally, they could perform a correlation analysis to examine the
relationships between the expression levels of each pair of these three genes in GBM cells.
3. The authors concluded that USP10 expression is significantly higher than DTX3L in GSCs based on the qPCR results in
Fig. 2d. However, relative quantification in qPCR requires similar primer efficiencies for valid comparisons between different
primers. Did the authors test primer efficiency?
4. Fig. 3i: In the H&E-stained coronal sections with indicated GSC tumor xenografts, no tumor cells or areas were observed
in the shUSP10 groups in these two GSC xenograft models. Is this result representative? From the survival data and IF
staining in Fig. 3j, there should be tumor xenograft mass in the coronal brain sections in the shUSP10 groups. Were these
three each H&E-stained brain sections from the mice that were euthanized at similar time points? The authors should also
confirm USP10 knockdown and decreased SATB2 expression in the brain slices. The same concern applies to Figs. 4 and
6.
5. The authors reported decreased SOX2+ tumor cells in xenografts following USP10 knockdown, DTX3L overexpression,
or 5-WU treatment. Did they observe an increase in differentiated cells by IF staining of some neuronal or astrocyte markers?
What is the potential mechanism? Additionally, did SOX2 expression change after these treatments in vitro?
6. An in vitro ubiquitination assay using recombinant proteins and ubiquitin should be performed to confirm USP10 and
DTX3L as the deubiquitinase and E3 ligase for SATB2, respectively.
7. According to the DepMap Portal, USP10 is categorized as a common essential gene. Do the authors have evidence that
GSCs are more dependent on USP10 compared to differentiated counterparts or normal cells?
8. In Fig 6, do the authors have data showing that 5-WU can penetrate the blood-brain barrier? They should also
demonstrate a decrease in SATB2 and USP10 levels in 5-WU-treated tumors.
9. Can SATB2 overexpression rescue the effects of 5-WU treatment? In Fig 6, the authors have already established ectopic
expression of SATB2 GSC lines for this validation experiment.
10. Although the authors stated in the Methods section that they used both male and female animals, they did not stratify
their analysis by sex or mention whether similar results were observed in both sexes.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
SATB2 is a transcription factor shown to play a role in many types of cancer. In glioblastoma, SATB2 is
overexpressed compared to low-grade gliomas; however, its role in GBM development and progression is
poorly understood. In the manuscript titled USP10 promotes glioma stem cell maintenance and glioblastoma growth by antagonizing DTX3L-
mediated SATB2 ubiquitination, the authors identify the deubiquitinase USP10 and the E3 ligase DTX3L as key mediators
of SATB2 stability. Using an IP strategy, the authors show that USP10 and DTX3L directly interact with SATB2.The authors
demonstrate that USP10 and DTX3L are preferentially expressed in GBM GSCs, where USP10 can reverse DTX3L-
mediated ubiquitination of SATB2 and rescue it from proteasomal degradation. Furthermore, shRNA-mediated knockout of
USP10 inhibits GSC proliferation, reduces tumor growth, and significantly extends survival time in a xenograft model.
Conversely, forced overexpression of DTX3L inhibits GSC formation and proliferation, as well as the growth of GBM tumors
in vivo. Taken together, the authors effectively show that USP10 and DTX3L regulate SATB2 stability and GBM
proliferation.The mechanism of SATB2 regulation was subsequently shown to be due to K48-mediated ubiquitination at a
conserved lysine site (K266), leading to degradation. Building upon this, the authors utilize a novel inhibitor of USP10 to
induce SATB2 ubiquitination and degradation. Treatment of tumor-bearing xenografts with this inhibitor resulted in a
reduction in tumor burden and an increase in survival time. The authors propose a model in which USP10 overexpression in
GBM rescues SATB2, whereas USP10 inhibition promotes SATB2 degradation, ultimately reducing GBM growth.
Overall, this is a well-constructed study that strongly supports the authors' model. They follow a stepwise and logical
approach in confirming their hypothesis, and the data presented is of very high quality. The paper is well-written, will be of
broad interest, and I commend the authors on their work.
Some minor comments
In Figure 8, the authors show that WU5 can inhibit GBM growth. Do the authors know if WU5 induces apoptosis?
Sticking with Figure 8, the authors show that WU5 effectively induces ubiquitination of SATB2, as expected. However, the
observed reduction in USP10 is potentially interesting. The authors mention that this was observed in a previous study, but
the mechanism remains unclear. Since MG132 is added to the media, proteasomal degradation cannot be the cause. Do the
authors know if WU5 affects USP10 transcription? Is SATB2 a transcriptional activator of USP10? Is USP10 also
ubiquitinated by DTX3L? It would be interesting to hear the authors’ perspective.
Minor typo on line 119: It should read "We first checked SATB2 protein levels."

Reviewer #1-Major points: 5. The molecular mechanism underlying SATB2 degradation by Wu-5 treatment
remains unclear. Both USP10 inhibition and the downregulation of USP10 protein level could lead to
increased ubiquitination of SATB2 by DTX3L, ultimately resulting in its degradation. The authors should
provide further clarification to distinguish between these possibilities.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. Previous studies have demonstrated that 1–
5 μM Wu-5 had no effect on USP10 protein levels, while 10 μM markedly reduced USP10 protein levels in
acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and breast cancer cells7, 8. To clarify its effect in GSCs, we performed time-
and dose-dependent experiments. Our results revealed that both USP10 and SATB2 levels decreased in a
time-dependent manner following treatment with 16 μM Wu-5, with an initial reduction at 12 hours and
7
further progressive declines at 24, 36, and 48 hours (Please see Figure R6a below). Moreover, treatment
with 8 and 16 μM Wu-5 for 24 hours dose-dependently reduced USP10 and SATB2 protein levels,
whereas lower concentrations (2 and 4 μM) had no significant impact on either protein (Please see Figure
R6b below). These findings indicate that USP10 and SATB2 protein levels decrease in parallel in a dose-
and time-dependent manner upon Wu-5 treatment in GSCs. Furthermore, cell viability assay revealed that
8 and 16 μM Wu-5 also dose-dependently inhibited GSC growth, whereas lower concentrations (2 and 4
μM) showed no significant effect (Please see Figure R6c below). Previous study has demonstrated that
Wu-5 exhibits inhibitory activity at low micromolar concentrations (1.5-3 μM)7. However, the lower
concentrations tested (2 and 4 μM) proved ineffective in our GSC model, likely because USP10 protein
levels showed no reduction under these conditions. Taken together, these results suggest that the
reduction in USP10 protein levels, rather than mere enzymatic inhibition without affecting protein
abundance, is likely the primary mechanism driving SATB2 degradation and the subsequent inhibition of
GSC growth induced by effective concentrations of Wu-5.

In this manuscript, Guo et al. investigated the mechanisms regulating SATB2 expression in glioma stem
cells (GSCs) and, for the first time, identified USP10 as a deubiquitinase and DTX3L as an E3 ligase for
SATB2 in GSCs. The authors also determined that K266 is the lysine residue regulated by these two
proteins. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated that USP10 is essential for GSC self-renewal and
tumorigenesis in vivo, with its effects being rescued by the overexpression of SATB2. The authors
identified YY2 as the upstream transcription factor mediating USP10 upregulation in GSCs. Lastly, they
assessed the therapeutic potential of the USP10 inhibitor Wu-5 in a glioma mouse xenograft model,
highlighting the translational promise of this project. Overall, this study is well-designed with appropriate
controls. The data are of high quality and robust in supporting the main conclusions, though additional
evidence is needed in certain areas, as outlined below. The manuscript is well-prepared, with clear
descriptions and detailed information. Moreover, the authors need to address the following comments to
further strengthen this study. The current enthusiasm for this manuscript is high.
Response: We are grateful for the reviewer’s positive comments and appreciate the concerns and
suggestions raised. In response, we have conducted extensive additional experiments to address these
concerns. We believe that the current manuscript has been significantly improved through these efforts
and the constructive feedback provided.

not contradict the findings in this manuscript.

SATB2 is a transcription factor shown to play a role in many types of cancer. In glioblastoma, SATB2 is
overexpressed compared to low-grade gliomas; however, its role in GBM development and progression is
poorly understood. In the manuscript titled USP10 promotes glioma stem cell maintenance and
glioblastoma growth by antagonizing DTX3L-mediated SATB2 ubiquitination, the authors identify the
deubiquitinase USP10 and the E3 ligase DTX3L as key mediators of SATB2 stability. Using an IP strategy,

USP10 and DTX3L are preferentially expressed in GBM GSCs, where USP10 can reverse
DTX3L-mediated ubiquitination of SATB2 and rescue it from proteasomal degradation. Furthermore,
shRNA-mediated knockout of USP10 inhibits GSC proliferation, reduces tumor growth, and significantly
extends survival time in a xenograft model. Conversely, forced overexpression of DTX3L inhibits GSC
formation and proliferation, as well as the growth of GBM tumors in vivo. Taken together, the authors
effectively show that USP10 and DTX3L regulate SATB2 stability and GBM proliferation.The mechanism
of SATB2 regulation was subsequently shown to be due to K48-mediated ubiquitination at a conserved
lysine site (K266), leading to degradation. Building upon this, the authors utilize a novel inhibitor of USP10
to induce SATB2 ubiquitination and degradation. Treatment of tumor-bearing xenografts with this inhibitor
resulted in a reduction in tumor burden and an increase in survival time. The authors propose a model in
which USP10 overexpression in GBM rescues SATB2, whereas USP10 inhibition promotes SATB2
degradation, ultimately reducing GBM growth.
Overall, this is a well-constructed study that strongly supports the authors' model. They follow a stepwise
and logical approach in confirming their hypothesis, and the data presented is of very high quality. The
paper is well-written, will be of broad interest, and I commend the authors on their work.
